title: Detection of imperative and declarative question–answer pairs in email conversations
research_question: Can sentence-level methods detect interrogative, imperative, and declarative questions and pair them with answers in email threads with better precision and recall than earlier methods?
methodology: Assume preassembled email threads; compare Naïve question-mark detection, a transferred POS/Ripper S&M detector, and Regex using about 50 handcrafted patterns. Compare eight listed Q–A methods: three paragraph-based SMQA variants, Naïve type matching, Random candidate selection, and sentence-based hand-weighted Heuristic, Ripper Heuristic-C, and linear-regression Heuristic-LR. Features combine lexical similarity, WordNet similarity, named entities/expected answer types, candidate order, addressee and thread position. Test question detection on a balanced Enron/CSpace sentence sample and pairing on separately annotated thread datasets using SM/LCS matching. See topic02 for exact populations, constraints and discrepancies.

key_findings.finding: In the mixed Enron/CSpace question-detection sample, about 80% of 350 annotated questions were interrogative, 11% imperative, 5% declarative, and 4% other; these are sampled question-form proportions, not mailbox prevalence.
key_findings.quote: 350 questions, about 80% were marked as interrogative, 11% as imperative, 5% as declarative and 4% as other.

key_findings.finding: On the balanced 700-sentence Enron/CSpace test set (350 questions of all forms and 350 non-questions), non-learning Regex reports precision 0.959, recall 0.860, F1 0.907, and mean 0.227 ms/sentence; non-learning Naïve reports 0.958/0.786/0.863. All 700 sentences were test data. Timing used Java 1.6 on an Intel Core 2 Quad 2.33 GHz with 3.25 GB RAM and Windows XP. This measures sentence question detection, not pairing or Topic assignment.

The paper specifies zero or one selected answer sentence per detected question for the Heuristic variants: choose the highest-scoring/most probable eligible candidate only above a threshold (default 0.5), and cap reuse of an answer at two questions by default. Candidates must be content sentences in a later message, from a different sender, in that individual’s first reply to the question email, and not detected questions. Content excludes quoted text, greetings, and signatures. These are stated prediction constraints; they do not establish gold link cardinality, realized reuse frequencies, or comparative semantic adequacy.
key_findings.quote: We attribute the highest-scoring or most probable candidate (appropriately) as the answer to a given question, assuming that the score or probability is above a minimum threshold (default 0.5). Finally, we limit the number of questions to which an answer can be assigned; for the experiments reported, we use a default value of two.

additional_evidence.quote: We examine each content sentence for questions, i.e., each original sentence that is not classified as a greeting or signature line.

A candidate answer is a content sentence in a subsequent message in the thread that is: (1) not from the sender of the question email, and (2) an individual’s first reply to the question email, [3] and (3) not one of the detected question sentences.
Given an email thread, the algorithm iterates through each original (i.e., unquoted) sentence [2]

key_findings.evidence_scope: Source-described methodology, explicitly present in the paper. The contract label unsupported means that comparative empirical proof of the constraints’ semantic adequacy is absent; it does not mean the algorithm description is missing.

key_findings.finding: For Annotator 1, Heuristic-LR reports LCS pair P/R/F1 0.5150/0.4857/0.4982 and SM pair P/R/F1 0.6211/0.5882/0.6021. For Annotator 2, corresponding scores are 0.6236/0.5240/0.5670 and 0.5725/0.3908/0.4597. Each annotator supplied about 90 Enron/CSpace threads containing Q–A pairs. The stated protocol is five-fold cross-validation separately per annotator and 50 experiment replications; explicit fold allocation unit, pair counts, and aggregation weights are not supplied. These are separate Q–A matching results, not Topic performance.

Gold segment extent varies by annotator: Annotator 1 favored short single-sentence Q/A segments; Annotator 2 favored longer segments. The proposed algorithms extract only individual sentences. This observes annotation-unit mismatch but does not compare sentence, clause, EDU, and arbitrary-span methods under controlled conditions.
key_findings.quote: notator 2 tended to mark longer segments (our algorithms extract only sentences as questions and answers, not longer pieces of text).

key_findings.finding: R05 describes SM as paragraph-based Q–A evaluation inherited from S&M; its related §3.2 training description marks a paragraph by containment of at least one annotated question/answer sentence. R05 does not restate a complete SM matching/counting rule. LCS instead explicitly matches word substrings: the longest common substring must exceed half the shorter segment, separately for both Q and A. This is tolerant pair matching, not exact-span F1, token IoU, or preservation of all decision-bearing text; the claim that it is more stringent is the authors’ characterization, not proof of a universal ordering between SM and LCS scores.
key_findings.quote: Two text segments are considered the same under LCS if the length of their longest common substring is greater than half the length of the shorter segment.

additional_evidence.quote: The first metric we employed is the paragraph-based metric used by Shrestha and McKeown [34], which we will call SM.

For training purposes, a paragraph is considered a question segment if it contains a sentence marked by the human annotator as a question, and a paragraph is considered an answer segment to a question paragraph if it contains at least one sentence marked by the human annotator as an answer to the question.
We consider two Q–A pairs to be the same if their question segments are the same by LCS and their answer segments are also the same by LCS.

key_findings.evidence_scope: Source-described metric specification. Definitions are present; comparative empirical proof of semantic completeness or universally stricter scoring is absent.

key_findings.finding: In qualitative sensitivity reports on their Enron/CSpace Q–A dataset, the authors say allowing later replies helps in some cases at higher runtime, a cap of three questions per answer is best overall, and a 0.8 threshold improves Heuristic-LR over the 0.5 default. This paragraph does not identify the exact subset, sample counts, fold-specific tuning protocol, or numerical deltas. These reports do not measure gold cardinality or work-text preservation.
key_findings.quote: Varying the heuristic on the number of questions to which an answer may pertain can modestly increase _F_ 1 -score; the best overall setting on our dataset is 3.
key_findings.evidence_scope: Author-reported qualitative experiment; no quantified comparative effect or fully specified tuning/evaluation protocol.

key_findings.finding: For Heuristic-C and Heuristic-LR on the Enron/CSpace Q–A data, the authors report convergence around 30 training threads under SM and LCS (Figures 1–2). The general individual-annotator experiment uses about 90 threads per Annotator 1/2, five-fold CV, and 50 replications; the curve paragraph does not specify which annotator data, exact held-out sample, or resampling procedure generated these plots. Curves vary and have standard-deviation bars. This qualitative source report does not establish a sufficient training-data size for a new domain or for Topic assignment.
key_findings.section: PDF page 11, §4.3 Learning and features; Figures 1–2
key_findings.quote: learning converges for both variants with a training set of approximately 30 threads.
key_findings.evidence_scope: Author interpretation of plotted Q–A learning curves; exact curve protocol and a formal convergence criterion are not reported.

limitations: No Topic segmentation, overlap/discontinuity assignment or work-text preservation evaluation (topic02.not_evaluated_for_msgloom).
Sentence-only Q–A predictions can differ from longer human-selected gold segments (R05-F05).
Candidate pruning and answer-link cardinality caps are heuristics; qualitative sensitivity results have no reported deltas (R05-F03/F07).
Balanced detection data, small pairing samples, annotator variation and unreported fold/duplicate controls limit generalization (topic02 split and annotation fields).
No separate pairing scores by interrogative, imperative or declarative question form (§4.3); combined improvements do not establish non-interrogative-specific pair gains.

Confirmed source discrepancies and assumption-dependent numerical inconsistencies are recorded in R05-I01–I06. R05-I07 is incomplete gold construction, and R05-I08 is a qualified filter-risk statement, not a demonstrated source contradiction.
Feature effects and convergence are incompletely quantified; no statistical test or p-value accompanies significance wording.

confidence_definition: Confidence in faithful extraction and stated evidence scope, not probability of deployment correctness. The contract uses supported for experimental backing. F03/F06 retain unsupported for lack of comparative empirical proof of semantic adequacy; their methodological statements are explicitly present and directly quoted. F07/F08 are source-reported qualitative empirical observations with incomplete protocols, not quantified guarantees.
raw_claims: Our hand-crafted database contains approximately 50 patterns.
The Heuristic algorithms for Q–A pairing extract sentences as questions and answers.

evaluated: Binary sentence question detection, including imperative and declarative forms
Extraction and linking of question–answer segments across messages in preassembled email threads; answer detection is embedded in pairing
evaluated_tasks.relation_to_ten_tasks: Supports the action/question/reply-scope extraction family only through question detection and Q–A links; complete reply scope and action scope are not evaluated. No Topic segmentation, labeling, classification, or span-assignment experiment.

annotation_unit.statement: Question detection: sentence with question/non-question label and question-form category. Pairing: human-selected Q/A segments of varying length; paragraph-level agreement and paragraph conversion for S&M. Annotator 1 favors single sentences; Annotator 2 longer segments. No supplied offset-level guideline establishes arbitrary spans, EDUs, or discontinuous gold units.

prediction_unit.statement: Regex/Naïve/S&M question detection classifies sentences. Proposed Heuristic variants return individual question and answer sentences; SMQA variants pair paragraphs. Comma-delimited phrase matching is a detection feature, not a predicted clause boundary or Topic span.

contiguity.statement: Each proposed Q or A endpoint is a contiguous sentence. Pair edges can connect nonadjacent messages in an already assembled thread. No global contiguous Topic partition, interleaved Topic clustering, or cross-thread Topic identity model is evaluated.

label_cardinality.gold: Binary question/non-question per detection sentence; question form separately marked as interrogative/declarative/imperative/other. Q–A gold link cardinality, many-to-many allowance and frequency are not specified; no Topic labels. Variable-length Q/A annotation does not imply any particular number of links per question or answer.
label_cardinality.prediction: One binary question decision per sentence; Heuristic gives zero or one selected answer per detected question, and at most two questions per answer by default. A cap of three is reported best overall in a qualitative sensitivity experiment. SMQA accepts candidate paragraphs over 0.5; SMQA-highest selects the most probable one. Naïve pairs an answer sentence to at most one question. These are configured limits, not measured realized degrees. Tie-breaking and conflict resolution when a reuse cap is reached are not specified.

gold.within_one_message: Not reported for one Q, A, or Topic; longer annotated segments do not establish discontinuous spans.
gold.thread_level: Questions and corresponding answers are annotated across thread messages; nonadjacency frequencies and formal gold discontinuity rules not reported.

prediction.within_one_message: Unsupported for a single multi-span Q, A, or Topic; each Heuristic endpoint is one sentence.
prediction.thread_level: A Q–A relation can connect a question to an eligible later message, with intervening messages allowed. This is nonadjacent relational linkage, not representation of one discontinuous Topic.

overlap.gold: Not reported: no gold many-to-many counts or overlapping Topic spans.
overlap.predicted: The specified Heuristic reuse cap permits the same answer sentence to be an endpoint in up to two Q–A relations by default. This is an algorithmic allowance, not a reported frequency of realized reuse or an overlap-specific empirical result. It does not establish multiple Topic memberships.
overlap.scope: Answer endpoint reuse across Q–A relations only.

dataset_domain.statement: English email from Enron senior management and CSpace MBA simulated companies. Paper describes cleaned Enron as about 30,000 threads/~150 users; CSpace as 2,739 threads/~275 users collected over a 14-week course. Those are corpus counts, not experimental sample counts. BC3 is discussed but not used for the reported tests. Business-email relevance is direct for Enron and qualified for simulated student companies.

annotation_process.question_detection: One human examines a random pool of 10,000 Enron/CSpace sentences until 350 questions are marked; 350 passed-over non-questions are randomly added. Exact number examined, per-corpus allocation and annotator instructions are absent. Question-form proportions are in R05-F01.
annotation_process.pairing: Four humans mark questions and corresponding answers if any. Annotators 1 and 2 each annotate about 90 threads with Q–A pairs; other annotators annotate significantly fewer. Shared-thread counts: all four 23; Annotators 1 and 2 61. Pair counts, adjudication and annotation release are not reported. Pairing annotators do not distinguish question forms. The 23 and 61 figures count jointly annotated threads, not agreed Q–A pairs.

results.metric: Fleiss kappa explicitly named for question-paragraph identification; paragraph-linking value called kappa without separately repeating the subtype
results.population: Four annotators; reported alongside the 23 Q–A threads annotated by all four. The paragraph/item counts used in each kappa calculation are not reported.
Annotators 1 and 2; reported alongside their 61 jointly annotated Q–A threads. Item counts are not reported.

inter_annotator_agreement.limits: The explicitly named four-annotator tasks are question-paragraph identification and paragraph linkage. The two-annotator results are described as question detection and Q–A pairing without a new unit definition. No contingency tables, item counts, or confidence intervals are given. Do not reinterpret these kappa values as exact-span, Topic, overlap, discontinuity, or preservation agreement. The separate sentence/question-form detection set uses one annotator and has no IAA.

split_and_leakage.question_detection: All 700 sentences used for testing. Regex/Naïve need no training. S&M keeps prior telephone-speech training; not retrained on email. Pattern-development separation from test collection is not documented.
split_and_leakage.pairing: Five-fold CV separately per Annotator 1/2 dataset, experiments replicated 50 times. Thread datasets are described, but explicit fold allocation unit, per-fold sizes, seeds, class counts and averaging method are not reported. Figures use number of training threads. Do not assert independent pair or thread fold assignments. The 23/61 shared-thread counts are annotation overlap, not train/test fold counts. Tables 7–8 and the curve/sensitivity analyses do not restate enough protocol to transfer the individual-annotator CV details to those results unconditionally.
split_and_leakage.duplicate_controls: Not reported: author/thread overlap handling across folds, quoted/near-duplicate train–test controls, temporal holdout, corpus holdout, or separation of hand-tuning from evaluation. Excluding quoted text from candidate answers is preprocessing, not evidence of leakage control.

definitions.question_detection: Reported precision, recall and F1 at sentence level. Standard interpretation: precision denominator is predicted questions; recall denominator is annotated questions. TP/FP/FN are absent. The source misnames F1 as geometric mean (R05-I01). Standard F1 is the harmonic mean 2PR/(P+R). R05 explicitly prints geometric mean; arithmetic checks do not establish its unreported implementation or aggregation for every table.
definitions.LCS_pair_matching: Longest common substring of words, not subsequence. Match iff its length is strictly greater than half the shorter segment; both Q and A must match. Pair precision/recall refer to predicted/reference pairs. Counts, handling of multiple matches and macro/micro aggregation are absent. The authors call LCS more stringent, but different units, denominators, matching rules, or realized predictions prevent a universal score-order claim. SM and LCS values must remain separate.
definitions.SM_pair_matching: R05 §4.3 identifies SM as the paragraph-based Q–A metric of Shrestha and McKeown [34], most suited to paragraph-segmented messages. Related §3.2 text defines S&M training labels by containment: a paragraph is a question segment if it contains an annotated question sentence; an answer paragraph contains at least one sentence annotated as an answer to the question. This training rule establishes paragraph granularity but is not a complete SM scoring specification. Exact projection of predicted sentences, pair matching, duplicate handling, and counting/aggregation are not restated in R05; do not infer exact sentence/span matching or substitute LCS for SM.
definitions.timing: Means per sentence for question detection; per thread for pairing. Java 1.6 on Intel Core 2 Quad 2.33 GHz, 3.25 GB RAM, Windows XP; no ARM or msgloom measurement. Table 9 internal inconsistencies prevent dependable latency inference.
definitions.non_equivalence: No Pk, WindowDiff, Topic pair/cluster score, exact span F1/IoU, whole-message multi-label score, or preservation metric.

material_inconsistencies.detail: PDF page 4 §3.1 explicitly calls F1 the geometric mean; no harmonic-mean definition is supplied there. For the Table 1 S&M interrogative-only Enron/CSpace detection test (350 non-questions plus the interrogative subset of the 350 questions; transferred telephone-speech training), printed P=0.623, R=0.865, F1=0.724. Applying the usual formulas to that one P/R pair gives harmonic mean about 0.7243 and geometric mean about 0.7341. The row is consistent with ordinary harmonic F1, not geometric averaging of that printed pair. This confirms a definition/ordinary-numerical-use mismatch; it does not prove the aggregation used for every table or license corrected values.
material_inconsistencies.disposition: Confirmed printed wording; ordinary F1 mismatch retained with scope. No guessed correction.

material_inconsistencies.detail: §4.3 says nine algorithms. Table 4 lists eight: SMQA, SMQA-regex, SMQA-highest, Naïve, Random, Heuristic, Heuristic-C, Heuristic-LR. Tables 5–9 likewise contain eight rows. No missing ninth method is inferred.
material_inconsistencies.disposition: Confirmed printed count mismatch; retain eight named methods and the source’s nine wording. No ninth method inferred.

material_inconsistencies.type: conditional runtime arithmetic inconsistency and unit ambiguity
material_inconsistencies.detail: PDF page 10 Table 9 prints mean/variance/median under a computation-times (ms) caption. Means/medians are SMQA 1800/2590, SMQA-regex 37.4/305, SMQA-highest 33.8/86.0, Naïve 1.10/0, Random 1.70/0, Heuristic 241/945, Heuristic-C 320/1340, and Heuristic-LR 316/1320. Assume each row describes the same population of nonnegative per-thread times, in the same units, with the arithmetic mean and ordinary median and the same observation weights (or one common empirical distribution), allowing ordinary printed rounding. Then median <= 2*mean; five rows (SMQA-regex/highest and all three Heuristic variants) violate this bound by much more than rounding. A single row’s means and medians computed on different samples or differently weighted aggregates need not obey that comparison, but such a construction is not described. If variance is conventional variance of those same times in ms^2, the median/mean separation also requires variance >= (median-mean)^2; even SMQA would require at least 624100 ms^2, not 5480. The caption does not supply correct squared units. Printed zero variances for Naïve/Random with positive means and zero medians are suspicious under literal same-population interpretation, but rounded zero alone does not establish exact zero variance. Preserve every printed value; units, aggregation, and intended corrections are unknown. The prose’s extremely-low-median description has no numerical threshold and is not independently a mathematical contradiction.
material_inconsistencies.disposition: Conditional inconsistency confirmed under ordinary same-population statistics; unknown source intent retained. No column swap, unit conversion, or decimal repair.

material_inconsistencies.detail: PDF page 9 Table 6, Annotator 2 Enron/CSpace Q–A data (about 90 threads, five-fold CV separately per annotator, 50 replications), prints Heuristic-C LCS P=0.5595, R=0.5018, F1=0.5439. Harmonic F1 of those P/R values is about 0.5291; their arithmetic mean is 0.53065. For each unit i, harmonic F1_i <= (P_i+R_i)/2; averaging all three metrics over the same units with the same nonnegative normalized weights preserves that bound. Printed 0.5439 exceeds it beyond four-decimal rounding. The row is therefore inconsistent with a single pooled P/R/F1 triplet or ordinary same-weight averaging of per-unit harmonic F1. Different weights, separately sampled runs, or mixed aggregation levels would invalidate that test; weights and per-run counts are not reported. Preserve the printed values rather than replacing F1 with 0.5291. Table 8 union-set SMQA-regex LCS P/R/F1=0.5324/0.4402/0.4471 and SM=0.5320/0.4398/0.4767 are also retained. Those cross-metric differences alone are not a proven error: averaged F1 need not equal F1 of averaged P/R, and matching populations or per-run distributions can differ.
material_inconsistencies.disposition: Table 6 conditional arithmetic inconsistency retained; Table 8 anomaly not promoted to contradiction. No inferred aggregation or numeric correction.

material_inconsistencies.detail: Table 7 bolds Heuristic SM precision 0.5118, although Heuristic-LR SM precision is higher at 0.5131. Values take precedence over bold emphasis; F1 ranking is unaffected.
material_inconsistencies.disposition: Printed emphasis mismatch retained; source range extended to include the higher value. No performance result changed.

material_inconsistencies.detail: The frozen papers/MANIFEST.json R05 entry and current frozen-corpus shortlist both name Chee Wei Kwong; the original local PDF page 1 author line names Helen Kwong and Neil Yorke-Smith. The manifest PDF hash matches the original PDF. Canonical analysis retains the PDF author line and records the metadata discrepancy. No external identity lookup, author-identity explanation, or manifest/shortlist edit is made.
material_inconsistencies.disposition: Confirmed local metadata/PDF mismatch; PDF author names retained. Identity cause not known.

material_inconsistencies.type: unreported operational gold construction; not a demonstrated contradiction
material_inconsistencies.detail: PDF page 8 states that all four annotators annotated 23 Q–A threads and calls these the intersection set; Annotators 1 and 2 shared 61 Q–A threads. These are shared-thread counts, not counts of agreed pairs. Page 9 refers to intersection and union sets described in [34]; page 10 Tables 7–8 use those labels without specifying how gold Q/A endpoints or pair agreements were merged, which annotators supplied each set, how disagreement was matched, or the pair denominators. R05 alone therefore does not establish all-annotator-agreed pairs versus any-annotator pairs as the exact scoring gold. Reference [34] was not consulted in this R05-only review. No precision/recall reversal or construction contradiction follows without fixed predictions, fixed counting rules, and the same evaluation population. Different datasets, denominators, training, or stochastic realized outputs can change the comparison.
material_inconsistencies.disposition: Retain as a source-detail gap. Do not infer gold set construction from the words union/intersection or from the 23/61 thread counts.

material_inconsistencies.type: source-described precision risk plus plausible recall/scope risk; not a contradiction
material_inconsistencies.detail: PDF page 5 footnote 3 explicitly says excluding an individual’s later reply can cost potentially reduced precision. That is logically plausible for this pipeline: pruning can remove a correct high-ranked candidate, change candidate-order/count features, change the selected answer, or interact with thresholds and reuse caps; downstream precision as well as recall can change. Removing true candidates can also cause recall or reply-scope loss, but that is an analysis risk inference, not a measured preservation result. Page 10 qualitatively reports improvement in some cases when this filter is removed, with greater runtime, but gives no metric-specific deltas, exact subset, or tuning protocol. Do not replace the source’s precision wording with an asserted recall correction.
material_inconsistencies.disposition: Prior terminology-defect implication removed. Preserve source wording and qualify plausible losses; no contradiction established.

interpretation.claim: A Q–A edge can help identify reply scope, but cannot establish that its endpoints are a complete work matter or that the whole thread has one Topic.

Sentence-only answers and the shorter-segment LCS denominator can accept a partial answer even if an omitted adjacent condition changes the decision. This is a plausible failure mode, not a measured result.

First-reply, author, and question-sentence exclusions can plausibly omit self-answers, clarifications, and later corrections. Candidate filtering can also change downstream answer ranking/selection and precision; it is not a recall-only operation. These are risk inferences, not measured work-scope loss or proof of an erroneous precision claim.
Binary question detection at a balanced prevalence and pair scores from one annotator cannot establish mailbox-scale Topic recall or safe approval coverage.

proposed_experiments.design: On user-reviewed synthetic or authorized representative work email, compare sentence, clause, arbitrary span and multi-span answer units with shared inputs and model conditions. Annotate necessary conditions, evidence and reply scope separately. Evaluate exact span/IoU, Q–A links and scope preservation as distinct outcomes.

Annotate shared-answer cardinality and within-message discontinuity explicitly. Compare unrestricted candidate links against first-reply, same-author and question-sentence filters. Include forked replies, self-corrections and questions answering questions; score gold and predicted memberships separately.

Use thread-grouped, near-duplicate-controlled held-out tests at natural question prevalence; report question-form detection, pair matching, complete scope recall and false scope expansion separately. Test runtime locally on ARM only after correctness is established.
